doc.title: John Fedchock interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 28, 2015

chapter: Making a living in New York
title: Cancelling a gig for a better offer: two times he had to
summary: He tells of dropping a small-college concert for a tour and a European residency for a Broadway revue before his wedding.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: How often do you have to — or do you — you have one thing on some date and someone offers you ten days and that thing is right in the middle of it. Do you ever have to call someone and say look I told you I was going to do this thing but now I’ve got this opportunity —

I’ve had a couple of times. One time was a long time ago I had a concert at a very small college and it was just that, it was in the middle of something. I got offered like a 10-day tour or something, that paid a lot of money. And so I called up the school and it was well in advance. I called up the school and I said, “look, I have this opportunity. I’d like to do it. Here are some people I would highly recommend. They’re all trombone players. They all do what I do. They write, and they would fit right in. They could even probably play the music you’ve been rehearsing of mine. They know my music and they’re well enough known.” This was a long time ago. I wasn’t very well known. And so I worked out all the details for them. And I said, “look if there’s a problem with the fee I’ll make up the difference.” Whatever. And then I took the other gig. And then the other one was one that I had a very nice gig at a school in Europe. It was like a week-long residency with a concert at the end. And it was going to be a lot of work but I was looking forward to it, because it was a very prestigious program. But then I got called — this is like three or four months before I was going to get married. And I got an opportunity for something in town that lasted like three months. And I felt bad enough leaving town for like twelve days or something with my wife trying to plan the wedding and everything. And at the same time we’re buying a house and moving and all that stuff. So I told — this was three months before their event I contacted the school and I said I have this opportunity here and I’m going to have to decline your offer. There were no formal contracts or anything. And they were a little upset about it, even though they had plenty of time and they did find someone to cover what it was I was going to do, and he did a great job and they were very happy. But there was a little bit of animosity there which I feel bad about, because I was very excited about doing it. But at the same time — and it turned out the opportunity I stuck around in New York for, it was like a revue. It was on Broadway but it wasn’t really a Broadway show, it was music, a music kind of revue, with a big band on stage and everything. And it paid New York Broadway scale so it paid pretty well. But it didn’t run as long as it was going to run. So I made about as much as I would have made doing the other gig and probably would have had more fun doing the other gig, but at the time it just felt like come on, you’re getting married, you’re buying a house, you’re moving, let’s be a responsible adult here and not just leave town for two weeks and leave your wife holding the bag. But those were the only two times I’ve ever had to deal with that.
